claims.claim: Dionysius was the bishop of Corinth in the mid‑second century, flourishing around AD 171.

Dionysius wrote a series of “Catholic Epistles” to many churches, including those of Lacedaemon (Sparta), Athens, Nicomedia, Gortyna in Crete, Amastris in Pontus, Cnossus, and Rome, as well as a private letter to a woman named Chrysophora.

His letters dealt with orthodoxy, refuted Marcionism, gave instructions on marriage and continence, urged charitable aid to the poor and to Christians condemned to the mines, and encouraged gentle treatment of repentant lapsers.

A fragment of his letter to the Roman church thanks the Romans for their longstanding custom of sending alms to needy churches and to prisoners in the mines, and declares that this mutual support unites the Roman and Corinthian churches founded by Peter and Paul.
Eusebius records that heretical groups attempted to falsify Dionysius’s letters by adding or omitting material, indicating the high authority his writings possessed in his own generation.
